header:
Date: 2025-06-18
Time: 16:00 PDT / 23:00 UTC
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Luis Martinez (Redwood SE), Karen Wu (Borealis CISO), Mark Redding (Borealis Head of Platform), Anita Sharma (Borealis DevOps)
Recording: Fireflies.ai auto-transcript
summary: Deep dive on Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) security architecture. Main topics: network isolation, ingress/egress controls, firewalling, KMS/HSM integration, audit logs and SIEM forwarding, SOC 2/ISO evidence. Borealis requires strict egress filtering, key management integration with HSM, and audit log retention for 7 years. Next steps: share artifacts, draw connectivity diagram, schedule pilot onboarding.
topics: Network isolation: VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs VPN/DirectConnect
Ingress/egress controls, firewalling, NAT and proxy patterns
Audit logs, SIEM integration, retention and tamper-evidence
Compliance: SOC 2 / ISO attestation and required evidence
transcript:
[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Samira from Redwood, AE on the account. Luis and I will run through the Private VPC security architecture and answer any compliance questions.
[00:09] Karen: Thanks, Samira. I wanted this session to be very network-ops and security focused - specifically ingress/egress and key management. We have strict egress rules.
[00:18] Luis: Yep, understood. We'll start high-level then drill into specifics like firewalling, NATs, and key ownership. Quick ask - Anita, do you have a list of current outbound destinations you can share?
[00:29] Anita: I can pull that, yeah. We'll have to check with corporate proxy, but I can get a dump.
[00:34] Mark: Also want to understand the options for connectivity: VPC peering, PrivateLink, or an IPsec VPN/Direct Connect. Latency matters for inference.
[00:44] Luis: Right. For Private we support a few patterns: 1) VPC peering into Redwood-managed VPC (if using cloud-hosted private), 2) AWS PrivateLink for endpoint-style connectivity, 3) Customer-hosted deployment where Redwood runs inside customer VPC or on-prem, 4) VPN/DirectConnect for on-prem network. Each has tradeoffs for egress control and network isolation.
[01:07] Karen: For Borealis, we prefer minimal outbound routes and a hub-spoke model. All egress must hit our proxy for data loss prevention. Can Redwood sit behind customer NAT/proxy?
[01:18] Samira: Yes. In Private deployments Redwood can be deployed inside your VPC so all outbound goes through your existing NAT/proxy stack. Alternatively, if using peering or PrivateLink, you can still force egress through your transit gateway with route tables. The key is that Redwood's control plane can be in our managed control plane but the data plane lives inside your VPC - that keeps egress under your control.
[01:39] Anita: That control-plane vs data-plane split - does anything leave our VPC to Redwood? Audit logs? Metrics?
[01:44] Luis: We can push telemetry and logs over an outbound TLS endpoint you approve, or we can write logs to customer-owned S3 bucket via VPC endpoint. For strict customers we offer an option to forward logs to your SIEM (Splunk/Datadog/SumoLogic) over your network. Nothing needs to egress to Redwood unless you opt in.
[02:03] Karen: Sounds good. On key management - can we bring our own KMS/HSM? We need customer-managed keys and HSM-backed signing for PII processing.
[02:12] Luis: Absolutely. Redwood Private supports CMK (customer-managed keys) via AWS KMS or external HSM integrations. We can either hold a key reference in the customer environment and perform crypto operations inside your network, or integrate with an HSM via PKCS#11 - the typical pattern is the Redwood runtime uses the local KMS to unwrap model artifacts and to encrypt/decrypt cache or persisted KV.
[02:33] Mark: Any latency penalty for KMS calls?
[02:36] Luis: Small - usually a few milliseconds per unwrap if using network KMS. For tight latency SLOs we recommend caching unwrapped keys in memory on the runtime with strict TTLs, and optionally using an HSM co-located on-prem to reduce network hops. We'll provide guidance and templates for TTLs and rotation.
[02:53] Anita: Rotation - who rotates keys and how do we ensure key compromise detection?
[02:58] Samira: We document key rotation processes and support automatic rotation patterns or manual rotation depending on your compliance needs. For compromise detection we rely on KMS/HSM audit logs (CloudTrail, PKCS#11 logs) and Redwood's audit streams; we can integrate both into your SIEM.
[03:12] Karen: SOC 2 - we're going to need evidence that access controls and RBAC are enforced. How does Redwood handle RBAC/SSO and admin access in Private deployments?
[03:21] Samira: Redwood supports SSO via SAML/SCIM provisioning and fine-grained RBAC. For Private, you can sync your IdP and control who has what role. Admin access to the runtime nodes should be restricted to your team's bastion host. We don't need SSH access into the nodes unless you want us to perform an engaged install.
[03:40] Mark: So for on-prem installs, is there an operator account Redwood uses? We want logs showing any Redwood engineer access.
[03:46] Luis: We always recommend using jump hosts and ephemeral access. When Redwood performs work, it is via customer-controlled access or an audited support channel. All support actions are logged and we can provide session logs.
[03:56] Karen: Audit log retention - regulator wants 7 years for certain events. Can Redwood retain logs that long or do we need to export to our systems?
[04:05] Samira: For Private we can write logs to a customer-owned S3 bucket or your SIEM; retention is under your control. Redwood's managed storage retention is shorter by default, so for multi-year retention we advise exporting to customer storage.
[04:16] Anita: VPC flow logs and application logs - how detailed are they? We need tamper-evidence for forensic purposes.
[04:23] Luis: We recommend enabling VPC Flow Logs, flow aggregation, and enabling object lock on S3 if you use S3 for audit storage. For tamper-evidence, use an append-only store and ship digests to your KMS or ledger. We can also sign logs before export.
[04:36] Karen: Are there any open ports required inbound to our VPC? We run strict host-based firewalls.
[04:42] Luis: Inbound from Redwood to customer is minimal or none. Typically, the models are served inside your VPC so inbound is internal. If you use PrivateLink, you create an endpoint service and we connect - all over the AWS fabric. For management plane calls, the control plane uses outbound TLS to our control endpoints; you can allow only specific FQDNs/IP ranges.
[05:00] Mark: FQDNs and IP ranges - do you publish a stable list?
[05:03] Samira: We publish an allowlist for dedicated/private customers and will share a CIDR/FQDN list. For strict customers we can also support using a proxy with mutual TLS so you only allow a single egress destination.
[05:16] Anita: Firewalling: Do you recommend stateful security groups + NACLs? We need guidance for enterprise patterns.
[05:22] Luis: Yes - security groups for instance-level controls and NACLs at subnet level. For egress we often put an egress-only NAT with proxy in the transit VPC, plus security group rules that only allow egress to the approved destinations. For on-prem, we recommend device-level firewall rules and an outbound proxy.
[05:38] Karen: What's the approach for vulnerability patching and host hardening?
[05:42] Samira: Redwood provides an ops runbook. For customer-hosted runtime we hand over a hardened AMI/container with CIS benchmarks applied; you run the patching cadence. For managed installs, Redwood patches and we provide patch logs and CVE reports.
[05:56] Mark: What about model artifacts storage? We want encryption at rest and access logs for any model download.
[06:02] Luis: Model artifacts are encrypted at rest. In Private we can store artifacts in customer-owned storage (S3 with SSE-KMS) or Redwood-managed encrypted storage. Access to artifacts is logged via CloudTrail or storage access logs. We can also require artifact signing so only signed model bundles load.
[06:19] Anita: A lot of our compliance questions center on egress - can we block all outbound except to our SIEM and KMS endpoints?
[06:26] Luis: Yes; if Redwood runtime is inside your VPC, you control outbound. We only need outbound to KMS (unless keys are local) and for control-plane telemetry if you enable it. You can block everything else. We document the minimal endpoints.
[06:38] Karen: For SSO provisioning and RBAC, SCIM support and group sync is critical. We also need audit trails of who made changes to model rollouts.
[06:46] Samira: SCIM is supported; we log role changes and can include those events in the audit stream to your SIEM. We'll show sample events in the next artifact.
[06:55] Mark: Any special firewall rules for GPU nodes or KV cache endpoints?
[06:58] Luis: GPU nodes communicate over internal ports; keep them in private subnets. KV cache traffic stays inside the VPC. If you split control plane, open only the necessary ports between control and data plane. We'll provide a default security group/template.
[07:12] Anita: Rate limiting - can we prevent accidental exfil via large model outputs? We want quotas at network/agent level.
[07:19] Samira: Redwood has per-route quotas and token limits; from a network perspective, you can egress-monitor and set alarms on abnormal outbound volumes. We'll collaborate on guardrails.
[07:31] Karen: What about encryption in transit? Mutual TLS between components?
[07:34] Luis: We use TLS between services; for customer-sensitive setups we can require mTLS using mutual certs via your PKI. We also support IPsec tunnels.
[07:44] Mark: Okay, let's talk about disaster recovery and backups - where are backups stored and how are they protected?
[07:49] Luis: Backups can be written to customer-owned storage with encryption and versioning enabled, and we recommend cross-region replication to your approved DR region. Access is controlled via IAM and KMS.
[07:59] Anita: Do you support SIEM connectors out of the box? We use Splunk.
[08:03] Samira: Yes, we have Splunk/Datadog/Sumo connectors and can forward logs via HTTP Event Collector or syslog over your gateway.
[08:12] Karen: Any compliance gaps to call out before we move to pilot?
[08:16] Luis: Nothing fundamental; it's mainly configuration choices - where the data plane lives, KMS model (customer-managed or managed), and log retention. For SOC 2 evidence we'll provide our own attestation plus configuration templates so you can demonstrate controls in your environment.
[08:29] Mark: Great. Can you share the hardening checklist and the exact CIDR ranges?
[08:33] Samira: Yes - I'll share the Private deployment checklist, hardening guide, and our allowlist. Anita, if you can send the firewall rules that will let us map recommendations.
[08:43] Anita: Will do. Expect an export by Monday.
[08:46] Karen: One more - does Redwood sign any of the audit data or provide integrity proofs?
[08:50] Luis: We can sign exported logs or provide signed digests. For high-assurance customers we recommend shipping digests into your KMS-backed ledger or S3 with object lock to ensure immutability.
[09:03] Samira: Okay we'll wrap with a quick recap. Action items: Samira to send SOC 2/ISO + allowlists and blank templates; Luis to draw network diagram and egress guidance; Anita to share firewall rules. We will then schedule the pilot onboarding.
[09:18] Karen: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[09:21] Mark: Thanks, chat after.
[09:23] Anita: Thanks.
[09:25] Samira: Thanks - we'll follow up with docs and a calendar invite for the pilot onboarding.
[09:30] [END]
